section.title: The Jews Triumph and Purim Established
section.sectionRationale: The dreaded day arrives, and the great reversal is complete: the very day the enemies of the Jews hoped to destroy them, the Jews prevail. They strike only those who attack them, refuse the plunder three times over, and rest. Out of the deliverance a feast is born. Mordecai and Esther write to establish Purim, so that every generation will remember how sorrow was turned to gladness and mourning into a holiday. The rescue becomes a permanent memorial.
section.thesis: On the day appointed for their destruction the people of God are delivered instead, and the deliverance is fixed forever in a feast of remembrance, sorrow turned to gladness by a hand no one can see.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the day of reversal and the victory of the Jews; the second day in Susa and the fall of Haman's house; and the founding of Purim as a lasting feast of remembrance.

units.label: The day of reversal
units.note: the appointed day of death becomes deliverance

verses.text: On the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, the month of Adar, the king’s command and edict were to be executed. On this day the enemies of the Jews had hoped to overpower them, but their plan was {{haphak|overturned}} and the Jews overpowered those who hated them.
In each of the provinces of King Xerxes, the Jews assembled in their cities to attack those who sought to harm them. No man could withstand them, because the fear of them had fallen upon all peoples.
And all the officials of the provinces, the satraps, the governors, and the king’s administrators helped the Jews, because the fear of Mordecai had fallen upon them.
For Mordecai exercised great power in the palace, and his fame spread throughout the provinces as he became more and more powerful.
The Jews put all their enemies to the sword, killing and destroying them, and they did as they pleased to those who hated them.

units.label: Susa and the house of Haman
units.note: the ten sons and the second day

verses.text: In the citadel of Susa, the Jews killed and destroyed five hundred men,
including Parshandatha, Dalphon, Aspatha,
Poratha, Adalia, Aridatha,
Parmashta, Arisai, Aridai, and Vaizatha.
They killed these ten sons of Haman son of Hammedatha, the enemy of the Jews, but they did not lay a hand on the plunder.
On that day the number of those killed in the citadel of Susa was reported to the king,

who said to Queen Esther, “In the citadel of Susa the Jews have killed and destroyed five hundred men, including Haman’s ten sons. What have they done in the rest of the royal provinces? Now what is your petition? It will be given to you. And what further do you request? It will be fulfilled.”
Esther replied, “If it pleases the king, may the Jews in Susa also have tomorrow to carry out today’s edict, and may the bodies of Haman’s ten sons be hanged on the gallows.”
So the king commanded that this be done. An edict was issued in Susa, and they hanged the ten sons of Haman.
On the fourteenth day of the month of Adar, the Jews in Susa came together again and put to death three hundred men there, but they did not lay a hand on the plunder.
The rest of the Jews in the royal provinces also assembled to defend themselves and rid themselves of their enemies. They killed 75,000 who hated them, but they did not lay a hand on the plunder.
This was done on the thirteenth day of the month of Adar, and on the fourteenth day they rested, making it a day of feasting and joy.

units.label: Purim established
units.note: the deliverance fixed forever in a feast

verses.text: The Jews in Susa, however, had assembled on the thirteenth and the fourteenth days of the month. So they rested on the fifteenth day, making it a day of feasting and joy.
This is why the rural Jews, who live in the villages, observe the fourteenth day of the month of Adar as a day of joy and feasting. It is a holiday for sending gifts to one another.
Mordecai recorded these events and sent letters to all the Jews in all the provinces of King Xerxes, both near and far,
to establish among them an annual celebration on the fourteenth and fifteenth days of the month of Adar

as the days on which the Jews gained {{nuach|rest}} from their enemies and the month in which their sorrow turned to joy and their mourning into a holiday. He wrote that these were to be days of feasting and joy, of sending gifts to one another and to the poor.
So the Jews agreed to continue the custom they had started, as Mordecai had written to them.
For Haman son of Hammedatha, the Agagite, the enemy of all the Jews, had plotted against the Jews to destroy them and had cast the {{pur|Pur}} (that is, the lot) to crush and destroy them.

But when it came before the king, he commanded by letter that the wicked scheme which Haman had devised against the Jews should come back upon his own head, and that he and his sons should be hanged on the gallows.
Therefore these days are called Purim, from the word Pur. Because of all the instructions in this letter, and because of all they had seen and experienced,

the Jews bound themselves to establish the custom that they and their descendants and all who join them should not fail to celebrate these two days at the appointed time each and every year, according to their regulation.

These days should be remembered and celebrated by every generation, family, province, and city, so that these days of Purim should not fail to be observed among the Jews, nor should the memory of them fade from their descendants.
So Queen Esther daughter of Abihail, along with Mordecai the Jew, wrote with full authority to confirm this second letter concerning Purim.
And Mordecai sent letters with words of peace and truth to all the Jews in the 127 provinces of the kingdom of Xerxes,

in order to confirm these days of Purim at their appointed time, just as Mordecai the Jew and Queen Esther had established them and had committed themselves and their descendants to the times of fasting and lamentation.
So Esther’s decree confirmed these regulations about Purim, which were written into the record.

haphak.gloss: To turn, overturn, reverse. This is the theme word of the whole book gathered into a single verb: the very day the enemies hoped to overpower the Jews was turned around, so that the opposite happened. Scripture uses the same word for God overturning cities and reversing fortunes, and here, though God is never named, the reader is meant to see whose hand does the turning.

nuach.gloss: To rest, to have relief from enemies. After the fighting the Jews rest, and it is this rest that becomes the heart of the feast. The word carries the biblical hope of the settled peace God gives His people once their foes are subdued, a rest that points beyond any single victory to the final rest secured for the people of God.

pur.gloss: The lot, a loanword the narrator pauses to explain, from which the feast of Purim takes its name. Haman cast the pur to fix the day of slaughter, treating the calendar as a game of chance; yet the very lot he trusted became the name of his enemies' rejoicing. Proverbs says the lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD, and Purim enshrines that truth in its very title.

basic.context: The day everyone dreaded finally comes, and it turns out the opposite of what Haman planned. Instead of the Jews being destroyed, they are able to defend themselves and their enemies fall. Notably, they strike only those who attack them and three times over refuse to take any plunder, even though the decree allowed it. Haman's ten sons are killed, and after the fighting the people rest and celebrate. To make sure this deliverance is never forgotten, Mordecai and Esther write to all the Jews and establish the annual feast of Purim, named after the lot Haman had cast, a yearly memorial of sorrow turned to joy.
basic.hermeneutics: The chapter raises hard questions: why so much killing, and how should we read the violence? The clues are that the Jews only defend themselves against attackers and repeatedly refuse the plunder, which sets them apart from mere revenge and greed. The key questions are what the threefold refusal of plunder signals, and why the deliverance had to be fixed in a permanent feast. The lesson is that a hidden God completes the great reversal and calls His people to remember His rescue forever.
basic.originalLanguages: The whole book is summed up in one verb here: haphak, to overturn. The day meant for the Jews' destruction was turned around. After the battle the Jews find nuach, rest, relief from their enemies, and that rest becomes the heart of the feast. And the celebration is named Purim, from pur, the lot Haman cast to fix the day of slaughter, the very lot that became the name of his enemies' rejoicing.
basic.typology: The day of doom turned into a day of deliverance foreshadows the great reversal of the gospel, where the day meant for death became the day of victory. The rest the Jews gained from their enemies points to the deeper rest secured for God's people. And a feast that fixes the memory of rescue forever anticipates the meal by which the church remembers her deliverance.
basic.christ: The reversal here, where the day of death becomes the day of life, is the pattern fulfilled at the cross and empty tomb, when the day the powers meant to destroy the Son became the day of their own defeat. The rest the Jews found points to the rest Christ gives, and the feast of remembrance anticipates the Lord's Supper, by which we remember a greater deliverance until He comes.
basic.god: God is never named, not even here where His people are so plainly rescued, and that reticence is deliberate. The reader is meant to see His hand in the overturning, the fear that falls on the enemies, and the timing of it all. The refusal of plunder, three times noted, shows a people acting under restraint, not greed. The hidden God completes His rescue and writes it into the calendar so it will never be forgotten.
basic.crossReferences: Proverbs 16 says the lot is cast, but its decision is from the LORD. First Samuel 15 recalls Agag the Amalekite, whose account is closed in Haman the Agagite. Psalm 30 turns mourning into dancing. And First Corinthians 11 gives the church a feast of remembrance until Christ comes.
basic.oneStory: The day appointed for the death of God's people becomes the day of their deliverance, and the rescue is fixed forever in a feast of remembrance. It is the gospel reversal in miniature, for the day the powers meant to destroy the Christ became the day of their defeat, and He has given us a feast to remember our rescue until He comes again.

context.literary:
Chapter 9 tells the same day three times and gives each telling a different job. Verses 1 to 5 announce the reversal in general terms across the empire. Verses 6 to 15 zoom into Susa, name ten dead men, report the king's third offer to Esther of whatever she asks, and grant a second day. Verses 16 to 19 return to the provinces with the total and explain why the villages keep the fourteenth of Adar while Susa keeps the fifteenth. Only then, from verse 20, does the writing begin to speak about the future. The narrator has carried the reader through a battle so that the reader can be handed a calendar.

Two narrative devices run through the chapter. The first is a refrain. Three times, in verses 10, 15 and 16, the report closes with almost the same words: they did not lay a hand on the plunder. The counter-decree had permitted plunder, 8:11, and the writer will not let the count of the dead be read without that sentence. The second is a word chain that begins in 9:1 with the reversal of the enemies' plan and comes back in 9:22 to describe the change from sorrow to joy and mourning to holiday. What happened on the battlefield and what happened in the heart are one event, narrated with one verb.

The listing of Haman's ten sons in 9:7-9 also has a literary function. Everywhere else in the story the enemy is a single figure with a single grievance. Here his whole house is written out name by name, as though the book were signing its ledger closed. In Jewish reading tradition the names are still recited together as a single list.

The second half of the chapter is a double authorisation. Mordecai writes the first letter, 9:20-22, and Esther joins him in a second, 9:29-32, so that the memorial rests on both of the book's central figures. The narrator inserts his own summary of Haman's plot in 9:24-25 and then closes the chapter with the sentence that Esther's decree was written into the record.
context.historical:
The date is fixed by the lot. Haman cast the pur in the first month, 3:7, and the lot fell on the twelfth, so the thirteenth of Adar was chosen almost a year in advance. Adar falls in late winter, and the fourteenth and fifteenth of that month were set apart in the years that followed. The book explains why two dates exist: the villages fought on the thirteenth and rested on the fourteenth, while Susa fought on the thirteenth and fourteenth and rested on the fifteenth, 9:17-19. Later Jewish practice still reflects that seam, keeping the fifteenth for cities that were walled. The custom of reading the book aloud at Purim and of fasting beforehand grows from the letter's mention of fasting and lamentation in 9:31.

The world of the story is the Persian empire in the twelfth year of Xerxes, whose court and provinces the book describes with unusual care. Thousands of Jews lived in that empire without a land or a temple, and their survival was the survival of the covenant people. The numbers reported, five hundred in the citadel and 75,000 in the provinces, are the largest figures in the book, and the text itself keeps them from turning into a triumph by repeating the refusal of plunder. To a first hearer, plunder would have been the ordinary reward of victory, and refusing it was a deliberate statement about the fight.

Haman is called an Agagite, and the first Israelites to hear this would have known the family. Amalek attacked Israel from behind at Rephidim, and the LORD swore to be at war with Amalek from generation to generation, Exodus 17:8-16. Moses told Israel to blot out the memory of Amalek once they had rest in the land, Deuteronomy 25:17-19. King Saul was later told to destroy Amalek, but he spared Agag and the best of the plunder, 1 Samuel 15:8-9, and lost his kingdom. Mordecai is the son of Kish, 2:5, the name of Saul's father, 1 Samuel 9:1. Some readers see a Benjamite finishing what a Benjamite left undone.
context.canonical:
Purim is the only annual festival in the Hebrew Bible that is founded by a human letter and not by a word from Sinai, and the book takes care to root it in older patterns of remembrance. Passover had been set as 'a memorial' and 'a permanent statute for the generations to come,' Exodus 12:14. Israel's feasts were to be joyful and open to the poor, the foreigner and the widow, Deuteronomy 16:11-14, and the gifts to the poor that Mordecai orders in 9:22 keep that tradition going. Nehemiah 8:10 will shortly say much the same to a restored community: eat what is rich, drink what is sweet and send portions to those who have nothing prepared.

The story is tied to the longest conflict in the Torah by the word Agagite. From Exodus 17 through Deuteronomy 25 and 1 Samuel 15, Amalek is the enemy who attacks the weak and the weary, and the book of Esther is the point at which Agag's descendant is brought before a court and the plot comes back on his head, 9:25. Psalm 7:15-16 describes the pattern in general, and Proverbs 16:33 says that the lot cast into the lap has its every decision from the LORD.

The New Testament takes up the two central motifs. The day meant to destroy God's people that becomes the day of victory is the shape of the cross, where the powers are 'disarmed' and 'triumphed over,' Colossians 2:15, and where the one who holds the power of death is destroyed by the death of Christ, Hebrews 2:14. The feast of remembrance meets its fulfilment when Jesus takes bread and cup and says 'do this in remembrance of Me,' and the church 'proclaims the Lord's death until He comes,' 1 Corinthians 11:24-26.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The author is writing to a community that has no state, no temple in view and no prophet speaking, and he wants them to leave the story with three convictions. The first is that their survival is not an accident of politics. The very day set for their death is the day of their victory, and the book keeps the reader looking at the calendar until that lands. The second is that the victory is theirs to guard. They are told to keep the memory alive in a family feast, in gifts sent to friends and to the poor, and in letters that pass from house to house, because a rescue forgotten is a rescue lost.

The third is how they should hold their strength. The threefold notice that they did not take plunder is the narrator's way of telling a people who had every excuse for greed that they fought for their lives and not for gain. He also writes with a warning tucked in: the list of Haman's ten sons is a reminder that the enemy who wants to erase a people ends by being erased. The book does not celebrate killing for its own sake. It celebrates that a people who were marked for extinction are still alive, at rest, and able to feast.

Underneath all of this is the author's steady silence about God. The rescue is described with the narrator's eyes only, and the reader is asked to carry the conclusion: no lot, no law and no legion has the last word over a people who belong to God.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The battle account is description. It reports what happened on one day in one empire under a specific edict. It nowhere tells God's people to take up arms against those who dislike them, and the New Testament teaches the opposite of retaliation: 'Do not repay evil for evil,' Romans 12:17, and 'my kingdom is not of this world,' John 18:36. What the church takes from the chapter is not a method of war.

The feast, on the other hand, is presented as a lasting instruction, and here the text becomes directive: the days are to be remembered by every generation, family, province and city, with feasting, joy, gifts to friends and gifts to the poor, 9:22 and 9:28. Christians are not bound to keep Purim, since the New Testament does not require it, but the pattern is clearly for imitation. Remember rescues by feasting, share what you have with those who lack, and make sure the next generation hears the story.

The refusal of plunder is also worth carrying over as an example. Believers are told elsewhere not to be motivated by greed, and the text quietly commends a restraint that Abram also showed when he refused the spoils of Sodom's king, Genesis 14:22-24.

debates.question: How should the scale of the killing be read: 500 in Susa, a second day of 300, and 75,000 in the provinces?

views.label: Defensive action against those who attacked, marked by restraint
views.case: The text says the Jews assembled 'to attack those who sought to harm them' in 9:2, and describes the victims as 'those who hated them.' The report of three refusals of plunder frames the whole account as a fight for survival. The large figures reflect an empire in which many were willing to act on the first edict, and the small figure for Susa's second day suggests a measured response.

views.label: A sobering record that the book reports and does not endorse
views.case: Others read the numbers as the ancient world's language of total victory and note that God is never said to command any of it. The extra day in Susa and the public hanging of Haman's sons at Esther's request in 9:13-14 sit uncomfortably beside the New Testament's teaching to overcome evil with good. On this view the book preserves an honest memory of how the rescue happened and leaves the reader to judge it in the light of Christ.

views.label: A literary and numerical presentation that should not be pressed for detail
views.case: A third group observes that the figures are given in an epic register, that the narrator stresses the totality of the reversal over the arithmetic, and that the book does not tell us how many of the dead had actually taken up arms. The safest conclusion, on this view, is that the chapter is more interested in the theological outcome than in a modern casualty report.

debates.bearing: All three agree that Esther 9 is a record of a unique deliverance and not a template for the church, and that the refusal of plunder is the book's own signal that this was a fight for life and not for gain.

debates.question: Does the label Agagite make Haman's allies into the Amalek that Israel was told to blot out?

views.label: Yes, Esther completes the Amalek story
views.case: Haman is called the Agagite again and again, and Agag is the king of Amalek whom Saul spared, 1 Samuel 15:8. On this reading Mordecai the Benjamite finishes what Saul left undone, and the refusal of plunder is a deliberate correction of Saul's sin, when he kept the best of the spoil, 1 Samuel 15:9.

views.label: It is a literary echo, and the enemies are simply those who hated the Jews
views.case: The text never says that the 75,000 were Amalekites, and the decree targets whoever attacks. On this view Agagite is the narrator's way of showing Haman's line of hostility, not of turning every enemy in the empire into a target of the ancient ban.

debates.bearing: The verse that matters is Deuteronomy 25:19, where the memory of Amalek is to be blotted out; Esther 9:28 sets the memory of God's deliverance against it. The link enriches the reading without requiring us to say that everyone in the story who died was an Amalekite.

study.originalLanguages:
The chapter's vocabulary is built on echoes that a careful reader can trace. Start with the first verse. The enemies had hoped to overpower the Jews, and the verb used means to rule over or to have mastery. The narrator then uses the same verb of the Jews: they overpowered those who hated them. The reversal is not only a change of fortune, it is a change of who does the ruling, and the same verb that describes Haman's ambition describes his enemies' victory. The verb that says the enemies' plan was overturned in 9:1 returns in 9:22, where the sorrow and mourning of the Jews are said to have been turned to joy and holiday. The book's key verb therefore appears once for the enemies and once for the people.

The refusal of plunder is worded with an idiom that has been echoing since chapter 2. The phrase 'they did not lay a hand on the plunder' uses the verb to send or stretch out, in the expression to lay a hand. Bigthan and Teresh in 2:21 sought to lay a hand on the king, Haman in 3:6 scorned the idea of laying a hand on Mordecai alone, and in 9:2 the Jews lay a hand on those who sought their harm. Now, in 9:10, 15 and 16, they do not lay a hand on the spoil. The same root gives the name of the festival's gift-giving, in 9:19 and 22, a sending of portions from one person to another. The hand that could have seized becomes the hand that sends gifts. That wordplay may be deliberate, and it is the moral of the chapter in miniature.

Memory is its own thread. The Hebrew for remember in 9:28 says the days are to be remembered and observed, and the memory of them shall not perish from their descendants. The same root sits in Deuteronomy 25:19, where Israel is told to blot out the memory of Amalek. And the verb that says these days should not fail, 9:27 and 28, is the same verb of passing that spoke of Persian law in 1:19 and 8:3: the law of Persia could not pass away, but neither will the memorial of God's rescue.

The name Purim is a foreign word, and the narrator glosses it twice, in 3:7 and 9:24, with the ordinary Hebrew word for lot. Verse 26 turns the foreign word into the name of a Jewish feast. The last phrase to note is 9:30, 'words of peace and truth,' a pair that the prophet Zechariah later joins in the command to love truth and peace, Zechariah 8:19. In 9:27 the phrase 'all who join them' uses a verb of joining that Isaiah 56:6 applies to foreigners who join themselves to the LORD.

typology.type: The day of doom that becomes the day of victory, Esther 9:1
typology.fulfillment: The day appointed for the destruction of God's people is turned round, and the enemy's own plan returns on his head, 9:25. The cross is the greater version. The rulers of this age crucified the Lord of glory, 1 Corinthians 2:8, and in doing what God's hand and plan had decided beforehand, Acts 4:27-28, they became the instrument of their own defeat, Colossians 2:15. Haman's fall was the fall of one man's scheme; the cross breaks the power of death itself, Hebrews 2:14-15. The parallel also breaks because Esther's rescue was won by the Jews' own arms, while Christ's was won alone, by suffering.

The Jews 'gained rest' from their enemies, and the rest becomes the heart of the feast. The Old Testament link is Deuteronomy 25:19, where Israel's rest in the land is the moment to blot out Amalek. In Christ that rest is carried further: 'Come to Me, all you who are weary,' Matthew 11:28, and a Sabbath rest that remains for the people of God, Hebrews 4:9-10. Esther's rest was in a foreign empire and lasted only as long as the king's favor. The rest Christ gives depends on His finished work and does not fade.

The Jews bind themselves and their descendants to celebrate these days in every generation, family and city. The pattern goes back to Passover as a memorial, Exodus 12:14. It reaches its fullest form in the meal Jesus gave: 'do this in remembrance of Me,' Luke 22:19, and 'you proclaim the Lord's death until He comes,' 1 Corinthians 11:26. Purim looks back to a rescue already done. The Lord's Supper looks back and forward, and the meal is anchored in a body given and blood poured out. The type falls short because Purim needed a decree from Mordecai; the Supper comes from the Lord Himself.

typology.type: Sorrow turned to joy and portions sent to the poor, Esther 9:22
typology.fulfillment: Mordecai's letter names two habits for the festival: joy and generosity, sending gifts to one another and to the poor. The church's joy, in Christ's words, comes after grief the way a woman's joy follows labour, John 16:20-22, and the generosity that flows from it echoes the one who, though rich, for our sake became poor, 2 Corinthians 8:9. Purim's gifts were a memorial of past relief. The gospel's are a response to a grace still being given.

study.christ:
Esther 9 does not mention Christ, and forcing it to would be a mistake. Neither Mordecai nor Esther is a disguised Jesus. What the chapter supplies is a pattern of deliverance that the New Testament itself uses when it explains the cross.

The pattern is the reversal of the appointed day. The book turns on a day that was chosen for a people's death and that ends in their rescue, with the enemy's plan coming back on his own head. The New Testament speaks in strikingly similar terms about the day of Christ's crucifixion. The rulers who crucified Him did not understand what they were doing, 1 Corinthians 2:8, and Peter says they did what God's hand and plan had decided beforehand, Acts 4:27-28. Paul says the powers that thought they had won were 'disarmed' and 'triumphed over' 'by the cross,' Colossians 2:15. The writer to the Hebrews says Christ's death destroyed the one who holds the power of death and freed those held in slavery by their fear of it, Hebrews 2:14-15. What looked like the enemy's triumph was the enemy's undoing. And the resurrection, in Peter's sermon, is God's answer to the day that was meant to end it, Acts 2:23-24.

The second pattern is rest. The Jews found rest from their enemies, and the day after the battle became a day of feasting. Jesus says 'Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest,' Matthew 11:28, and Hebrews says a Sabbath rest remains for God's people because Christ has finished His work, Hebrews 4:9-10. Esther's rest was short and earthly, but it was real, and it points to a deeper one.

The third pattern is the memorial meal. Israel is told to remember a rescue by a feast, and Jesus gives His church a meal to remember a greater one. The words 'until He comes,' 1 Corinthians 11:26, place that meal between a finished work and a coming day, and they suggest what Purim could only suggest, that the feast is also a sign that the story is not over.

A last resonance is in the letters of 'peace and truth,' 9:30. Christ is the one who says 'Peace I leave with you,' John 14:27, and who came full of grace and truth. Even here the picture is partial. The Jews of Susa won their day by the sword. Christ, who told Peter to put his own sword away, Matthew 26:52, won His by giving His life, and the peace He speaks is peace with God, not merely peace from enemies.
study.god:
The chapter's greatest claim about God is made without His name. The lot was cast in the first month, 3:7, by a man who trusted chance, and Proverbs 16:33 says the lot's every decision is from the LORD. A date was chosen by a pagan superstition and became the date of Israel's victory. The book asks the reader to see that nothing in the world, not even a rigged lottery, sits outside God's hand.

He is the God who hears cries and sets deliverance in motion long before it is seen. The 'fear of Mordecai' that falls on the officials, 9:3, and the 'fear of them' that falls on the peoples, 9:2, are the sort of quiet turning of hearts the Bible attributes to God, as when He promised Israel that no one would stand against them in Joshua 1:5. The people do their part, but the situation has been made favorable before they act.

He is the God of justice who lets the trap close on the trapper. The scheme comes back on Haman's head and on the heads of his sons, 9:25. Psalm 7:15-16 describes the principle: he who digs a pit falls into it. The chapter also shows how long God's memory is. Amalek's attack on Israel came centuries earlier, and the LORD had sworn to be at war with Amalek from generation to generation, Exodus 17:16. The Agagite thread shows that God's promises about judgment are not forgotten, and neither are His promises about blessing.

He values memory. The chapter commands that the days be remembered by every generation. God commanded Israel to blot out the memory of Amalek and to keep alive the memory of the rescue from Egypt, and this pair of commands works together. The book of Esther is itself an act of remembering, and worship in Scripture is often the act of telling the story again.

He is also a God who does not require His people to be bloodthirsty in order to be victorious. The refusal of plunder is the narrator's gentle rebuke to greed. Whether God endorses everything the Jews did in the day of battle is not said, and the tension is real. The God who commanded Amalek's end in the Torah is the Father of the Lord Jesus, who commands love of enemies, Matthew 5:44, and a reader should hold both truths together and not force the tension shut.

For worship, the chapter says joy is an act of obedience. Feasting, sending gifts, remembering the poor and telling the story to children are not extras. Nehemiah 8:10 says the joy of the LORD is His people's strength, and the Jews of Susa learned to make that joy visible on a calendar.

crossReferences.note: Haman, having decided to destroy the whole people, casts the pur in the first month to choose the day. That lot is the origin of the festival's name. The verse shows how the book turns the enemy's own instrument, a lottery, into the title of a feast of deliverance.

The counter-decree permits the Jews to defend themselves and to plunder their enemies. Chapter 9 reports that they took the first permission and refused the second three times. Reading the two verses together shows that the restraint was the Jews' own choice, not a limit imposed on them.

Esther's call to fast for three days before she goes to the king stands behind the mention of fasting and lamentation in 9:31. The festival that celebrates rescue also remembers the fast that preceded it, so that joy is never cut off from the prayer that came first.

After Amalek attacked Israel, the LORD told Moses to write it down and swore to be at war with Amalek from generation to generation. Haman the Agagite is the descendant of that enemy. The link puts the hostility of chapters 3 to 9 in the frame of a long-standing conflict and not a personal quarrel.

Israel is told to remember what Amalek did and, when God gives rest from all enemies, to blot out the memory of Amalek. Esther 9 speaks of rest from enemies, 9:16-22, and of a memory that must not fail, 9:28. The book sets the memory of deliverance against the memory of the enemy.

Saul spared Agag and kept the best of the spoil. In Esther the descendant of Agag is destroyed and the Jews refuse the spoil three times. Readers have long noticed the contrast, which invites the thought that what was lost by disobedience is here recovered by restraint.

Abram refuses to keep so much as a thread from the king of Sodom so that no one could say he had made Abram rich. The Jews of Esther 9 make the same choice with the same motive: victory that is not a source of profit is a victory clearly given by God.

A proverb about dice and providence, and the whole feast is a comment on it. The pur that Haman cast, trusting chance, gave its name to the people's celebration, which shows that even a rigged lottery falls under a Ruler who is never named in the book.

The wicked man digs a pit and falls into it, and his mischief returns on his own head. Esther 9:25 uses the same picture in narrative: the scheme Haman devised comes back on his own head, and he and his sons hang on the gallows he had prepared.

The governor tells the people to eat rich food, drink sweet drink and send portions to those who have nothing prepared, because the joy of the LORD is their strength. The counsel matches Mordecai's instruction for Purim in Esther 9:22, when joy is joined to gifts to the poor.

A Sabbath rest remains for the people of God, and whoever enters it rests from his own works. The rest that the Jews gained from their enemies in Esther 9:22 is a small earthly picture of the rest that God's people enter through Christ.

Jesus gives a memorial meal, and the church proclaims the Lord's death until He comes. The Lord's Supper does for the church what Purim does for the Jews: it fixes a rescue into a recurring meal so that later generations will not forget.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story begins with a promise that the serpent's line and the woman's line will be at war and that the woman's offspring will win, Genesis 3:15. Everything afterwards is the working out of that war. Amalek, who fell on Israel's stragglers at Rephidim, is one of its earliest fronts. Saul fails on that front, and Haman the Agagite is the last known descendant of the enemy on it. In Esther 9 the front closes. The people who were marked for extinction are alive, rested and feasting, and the promised line that leads to Christ has been kept safe in the Persian empire, exactly as the promise to Abraham needed.

The chapter also answers a question that lay over the exile: has God forgotten His people? The ten names of the dead, the count of the fallen, the refusal of plunder and the fixed dates of the feast are the narrator's way of saying that God has not. The rescue is hidden in the sense that no miracle occurs and no prophet speaks, but the calendar itself becomes a testimony. Every year the Jews would open the story again and say what had happened on the thirteenth of Adar.

The story then moves into Christ. The greater day appointed by the enemy was the day of the cross, and it too was turned round: the rulers 'disarmed' and 'triumphed over,' Colossians 2:15, the power of death destroyed, Hebrews 2:14. The church has her own feast, taken from the Lord's own hands, and she celebrates it 'until He comes,' 1 Corinthians 11:26. Her joy is not the joy of survival alone but of a resurrection.

The new creation completes what Purim only sketched. There the rest that Israel gained for a season is given forever, and every tear is wiped away, Revelation 21:4. The feast that began as a letter from a Persian court becomes the wedding supper of the Lamb, Revelation 19:9, to which people from every nation are invited. The enemy's lots and edicts are gone, and the memory of the LORD's rescue is not written on a calendar but lived in the presence of the one who wrote the story.

sermon.title: The Tables Are Turned
sermon.why: From Begg's series A Study in Esther, this message expounds Esther 9, the day of reversal in which the Jews are delivered and their enemies fall, tracing the unseen providence of God who turns the tables for His people; the founding of Purim in the same chapter is handled in the companion message of the series. A faithful, expository handling of this movement.

quiz.q: What happened on the thirteenth of Adar, the day set for the Jews' destruction?

options.text: The day was overturned, and the Jews prevailed over those who hated them.
options.note: Esther 9:1 states the enemies' plan was overturned; the reversal is complete.

options.text: The Jews were nearly destroyed but escaped at the last moment.
options.note: They were not nearly destroyed; the day was fully turned in their favor.

options.text: The king cancelled the day entirely and no fighting occurred.
options.note: The day still came, but the outcome was reversed; the Jews defended themselves.

options.text: Haman rose again to lead a final assault.
options.note: Haman was already dead; his plot recoiled and his people fell.

quiz.q: What detail is repeated three times to mark the character of the Jews' victory?

options.text: They did not lay a hand on the plunder.
options.note: Esther 9:10, 15, 16 all stress their refusal of spoil, a mark of restraint.

options.text: They spared every woman and child.
options.note: Restraint is emphasized, but the repeated refrain is specifically about the plunder.

options.text: They fought only at night.
options.note: There is no such detail; the repeated note is the refusal of plunder.

options.text: They asked the king's permission before each battle.
options.note: The threefold refrain concerns the plunder they refused, not repeated permissions.

quiz.q: Why was the feast of Purim established?

options.text: To fix the memory of the deliverance forever, so every generation would remember sorrow turned to joy.
options.note: Esther 9:27-28 makes remembrance the heart of the feast.

options.text: To celebrate Mordecai's rise to power in the palace.
options.note: The feast remembers the whole people's deliverance, not merely Mordecai's honor.

options.text: To mark the death of Haman's ten sons alone.
options.note: Their fall is part of it, but the feast commemorates the rescue of the whole people.

options.text: To replace the Passover with a new festival.
options.note: Purim did not replace Passover; it is a distinct memorial of this deliverance.

quiz.q: Where does the name Purim come from?

options.text: From the pur, the lot Haman cast to fix the day of slaughter.
options.note: Esther 9:24-26 explains the feast is named after the lot Haman cast.

options.text: From the Hebrew word for deliverance.
options.note: It sounds fitting, but the text names it from pur, the lot, not from deliverance.

options.text: From the name of the month of Adar.
options.note: The feast falls in Adar, but its name comes from the lot, the pur.

options.text: From the Persian word for feast.
options.note: The narrator explicitly derives the name from pur, the lot Haman cast.

quiz.q: How does the great reversal of this chapter point to Christ?

options.text: The day meant for death became the day of deliverance, fulfilled when the cross became the defeat of the powers.
options.note: 1 Corinthians 2:8 shows the day of the cross undoing the powers that sought it.

options.text: The killing of the enemies models how the church should treat its opponents.
options.note: The chapter is descriptive; Christ conquers by the cross, not the sword.

options.text: Mordecai's fame is a direct prophecy of Christ's kingship.
options.note: Mordecai's rise matters, but the christological center is the reversal of the day of death.

options.text: The chapter has no connection to the gospel.
options.note: The turning of the day of death into deliverance runs straight to the cross and resurrection.

questions: The day meant for destruction became the day of deliverance. Where in your life do you need to trust that God can completely reverse a situation that looks hopeless?
The Jews refused to take the plunder, again and again, even when it was permitted. Where might God be calling you to restraint, to want only what is right rather than all you are allowed?
Mordecai and Esther made sure the rescue would never be forgotten. What has God done in your life that you are in danger of forgetting, and how could you build in a way to remember it?
Purim turns a day of dread into a day of gifts to friends and care for the poor. How does remembering God's deliverance move you toward generosity rather than mere relief?
The lot Haman trusted became the name of his enemies' joy. Where are you tempted to fear chance and circumstance, when Scripture says even the lot is governed by the Lord?

translationNotes.note: The plan was overturned renders the Hebrew haphak, to turn or reverse, the theme word of the whole book gathered into a single verb at the moment of deliverance.

The refrain they did not lay a hand on the plunder, repeated in verses 15 and 16, is a deliberate structural signal of restraint, echoing and reversing Saul's seizure of Amalekite spoil in 1 Samuel 15.
The narrator pauses to explain the loanword Pur as the lot, from which the feast of Purim is named; the parenthesis is in the original.
